newsitem.title: USA: Geomagnetic storm ruffles Earth's magnetic field.
newsitem.headline: Geomagnetic storm ruffles Earth's magnetic field.

text.p: A geomagnetic storm reached Earth's magnetic field this month, raising questions about the death of a communications satellite, space experts said on Tuesday.

The storm, which started on Jan. 6 as a huge gaseous emission from the Sun's corona, arrived around Earth on Jan. 10-11, space-watchers at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said.

"We had no indication that this thing was coming right at us," said David Speich, a space scientist at NOAA. Only about 11 percent of such events, known to scientists as coronal mass ejections, aim straight at Earth, as this one did, Speich said by telephone.

Geomagnetic storms have affected satellite transmissions, power grids and pipelines in the past, but neither Speich nor other government experts would draw a direct link between the storm and the demise of an AT&T satellite, Telstar 401, which went silent last Saturday morning.
AT&T spokesman Mike Granieri said no specific cause had been found for the demise of Telstar 401.
"When we know we will tell the world," Granieri said by telephone from New Jersey. "... The last thing we'd want to see is for this to happen to somebody else."

Sophisticated NASA spacecraft captured images of the storm, a great magnetised cloud of solar particles lifting off the Sun and heading toward Earth, appearing as an expanding ring of light larger than the Sun, known as a halo event.
"The halo event says there's no way you can escape it: a billion tons of matter moving at 2 million miles an hour," Speich said from Boulder, Colorado.
He emphasised that most humans would have been oblivious while the event was occuring, because Earth's magnetic field tends to divert most of the charged particles.

But at the altitude where satellites do their work -- tens of thousands of miles (kms) about Earth's surface -- the magnetic buffetting could have been intense enough to cause large sparks across the surface of spacecraft or even to send magnetic particles through spacecraft, Speich said.
NASA's Don Savage also declined to make a connection between the solar event and the doomed satellite, but said, "We do know in the past that other spacecraft have been affected."
